References for Absorbed Dose Values (mGy/MBq)

Specific Absorbed Fraction

Absorbed Fraction · Specific Absorbed Fraction · Monte Carlo Calculation

1 Absorbed Fraction

The photon absorbed fraction $\phi$ is simply the fraction of the emitted photon energy by the source that is absorbed in the region of interest [1,2]. The absorbed fraction can only be determined after specifying the source and the geometry of the absorber, the photon energy, and the material medium [1].

The absorbed fraction can be expressed as the proportion of the photon energy emitted by the source that is absorbed by the target; this relationship is given by the equation below [1]:

$$\phi = \frac{\text{photon energy absorbed by target}}{\text{photon energy emitted by source}}$$

2 Specific Absorbed Fraction (SAF)

Once the absorbed fraction is obtained, it is possible to determine the Specific Absorbed Fraction (SAF) given the mass of the target; thus, the SAF is the ratio of the absorbed fraction to the mass of the target in kg⁻¹ [3]. This ratio is given by the equation below:

$$\Phi(r_T \leftarrow r_S, E_i, t) = \frac{\phi(r_T \leftarrow r_S, E_i, t)}{M(r_T, t)}$$

Where $\phi(r_T \leftarrow r_S, E_i, t)$ is the absorbed fraction (defined as the fraction of radiation energy $E_i$ emitted within the source tissue $r_S$ at time $t$ that is absorbed in the target tissue $r_T$), and $M(r_T, t)$ is the time-dependent mass of the target tissue $r_T$ in the reference individual [3].

References

  1. Brownell GL, Ellett WH, Reddy AR. (1968). Absorbed fractions for photon dosimetry. Journal of Nuclear Medicine Suppl :29-39.
  2. Howell RW, Wessels BW, Loevinger R, Watson EE, Bolch WE, Brill AB, Charkes ND, Fisher DR, Hays MT, Robertson JS, Siegel JA, Thomas SR. (1999). The MIRD perspective 1999. Medical Internal Radiation Dose Committee. Journal of Nuclear Medicine 40(1):3S-10S.
  3. Bolch WE; Eckerman KF; Sgouros G; Thomas SR. (2009). MIRD pamphlet No. 21: a generalized schema for radiopharmaceutical dosimetry — standardization of nomenclature. Journal of Nuclear Medicine 50(3):477-84.

1 SAF Calculation Method

The SAF values in this study were calculated from the energy deposited per unit mass, scored with a tally of the Monte Carlo code in the target region (any Monte Carlo radiation transport code can be used). Since the results are returned in Gy/source, which corresponds to J·kg⁻¹, it is therefore possible to calculate the SAF using the equation below:

$$\text{SAF}(r_T \leftarrow r_S) = \frac{D_{\text{MC},\, r_T \leftarrow r_S}}{E_{i,\, r_S}}$$

Where $D_{\text{MC},\, r_T \leftarrow r_S}$ is the absorbed dose obtained with the Monte Carlo code (energy deposited per unit mass, in J·kg⁻¹ per source particle), for a source-target organ pair, and $E_{i,\, r_S}$ is the energy emitted by the source organ in J.

2 Organs with Multiple Subregions

With this approach it is possible to calculate SAF values for various scenarios; however, some organs and tissues have more than one segmented region, such as the kidneys (cortex, medulla and pelvis). In these cases, the SAFs were obtained using the equation below, which represents a weighted average of the SAF values of each subregion of the corresponding organ/tissue:

$$\text{SAF organ}_{r_T \leftarrow r_S} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i}^{n} m_i \cdot \text{SAF}_{i,\, r_i \leftarrow r_S}}{M_{\text{Organ}}}$$

Where $M_{\text{Organ}}$ is the total mass of all subregions of the organ or tissue, $m_i$ is the mass of the subregion, and $\text{SAF}_{i,\, r_T \leftarrow r_S}$ are the SAF values obtained for the subregion. This approach was used for all organs/tissues that have subregions, or bilateral organs.

Reference phantoms

Human Anatomical Models · ICRP Publication 110 (Voxel) · ICRP Publication 145 (Mesh MRCP)

1 What is a Computational Phantom?

In radiation dosimetry and radiological protection, a computational phantom is a computerized, anatomical representation of the human body designed for use with Monte Carlo radiation transport simulation codes (such as PHITS, Geant4, MCNP, and FLUKA) [1,2].

Computational phantoms provide the spatial geometry, volume, density, and elemental composition (H, C, N, O, etc.) of organs and tissues. They enable physicists to simulate ionizing radiation interactions, energy deposition, and calculate Specific Absorbed Fractions (SAFs), organ absorbed doses, and effective dose quantities that cannot be measured directly inside living human beings [1,3].

  • Stylized Phantoms (1960s–1980s): Early mathematical models (e.g., MIRD-5, Snyder phantoms) represented organs using simple geometric equations (spheres, cylinders, cones, and ellipsoids). While computationally lightweight, they lacked anatomical fidelity.
  • Voxel Phantoms (ICRP 110, 2009): Reconstructed from three-dimensional medical tomographic images (CT and MRI) of real human subjects, partitioned into volumetric pixels (voxels).
  • Mesh-Type Phantoms (ICRP 145, 2020): Advanced boundary-representation models constructed from high-definition polygon and tetrahedral volume meshes, eliminating voxel artifacts and enabling micrometer-level target layering.

2 ICRP Publication 110: Reference Voxel Phantoms

In 2009, the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP), in a joint effort with the International Commission on Radiation Units and Measurements (ICRU), released ICRP Publication 110: Adult Reference Computational Phantoms [1]. This landmark publication established the official international voxel models for the:

  • Adult Reference Male (AM): Height: 1.76 m | Body Mass: 73 kg (composed of approximately $1.95 \times 10^6$ active voxels with dimensions $2.137 \times 2.137 \times 8.0\text{ mm}^3$) [1].
  • Adult Reference Female (AF): Height: 1.63 m | Body Mass: 60 kg (composed of approximately $3.88 \times 10^6$ active voxels with dimensions $1.775 \times 1.775 \times 4.84\text{ mm}^3$) [1].

These models were derived from high-resolution CT scans of real individuals and then systematically modified voxel-by-voxel so that organ masses and body dimensions strictly matched the standard physiological reference parameters recommended in ICRP Publication 89 [1,2]. Over 140 segmented tissues and organs were defined with specific elemental compositions and densities, providing the baseline for reference dose conversion coefficients in ICRP Publications 116, 119, and 133 [1].

3 Structural Limitations of Voxel Models

Although ICRP 110 provided a monumental leap in anatomical realism compared to stylized models, voxel-based geometry has fundamental constraints [1,4]:

  • Voxel "Stair-Stepping" Artifacts: Smooth, curved organ surfaces are approximated by discrete cubic blocks, producing artificial staircase-like boundaries that distort local surface doses and particle transport at tissue interfaces.
  • Inability to Model Microscopic Target Layers: Key radiosensitive target tissues often consist of extremely thin layers:
    • The skin basal layer ($50\text{–}100\,\mu\text{m}$ depth);
    • The lens of the eye sensitive regions (anterior subcapsular epithelium);
    • The target mucosal layer in the walls of the stomach, small intestine, colon, and urinary bladder.
    In a voxel phantom, resolving these micrometer-thick layers across the entire body would require billions of voxels, exceeding practical computer memory limits.
  • Rigid Posture: Voxel matrices are static grids and cannot be deformed or articulated into realistic working postures (e.g., seated, bending, or walking).

1 From Voxel to Mesh: The ICRP Publication 145 Paradigm

To overcome the fundamental limitations of voxel-based representations while maintaining total consistency with ICRP 89 anatomical reference data and ICRP 110 organ masses, the ICRP Task Group 103 developed the Adult Mesh-Type Reference Computational Phantoms (MRCPs), published in ICRP Publication 145 (2020) [1].

The MRCPs convert the voxel structures of the ICRP 110 phantoms into high-definition polygon surface meshes and internal volume-filling tetrahedral solid meshes (MRCP-AM for the Reference Male and MRCP-AF for the Reference Female) [1,2].

2 Key Innovations & Advantages of MRCPs

  • Smooth Anatomical Surfaces: By replacing cubic voxels with continuous polygon meshes, the staircase artifact is completely eliminated, accurately reproducing organic curves, tissue boundaries, and organ interfaces [1].
  • Direct Modeling of Micrometer-Thick Target Layers: For the first time, micrometer-scale radiosensitive stem cell layers are incorporated directly into whole-body reference phantoms:
    • The basal layer of the skin ($50\text{–}100\,\mu\text{m}$ depth) is modeled explicitly as a continuous sub-millimeter shell;
    • The eye lens is delineated into the anterior capsule, epithelial germinative zone, and nucleus;
    • The alimentary tract organs (esophagus, stomach, small intestine, colon) and urinary bladder include explicitly modeled mucosal layers and wall structures.
  • Organ Subregion Segmentation: Multiple subregions are segmented within complex organs (such as the renal cortex, medulla, and pelvis in the kidneys), providing detailed localized internal dosimetry.
  • Deformable Posture: Being surface mesh-based, the phantoms can be articulated and transformed into realistic non-standing postures (e.g., sitting, kneeling, or lying down) for occupational exposure scenarios [1,2].

3 Application in This Study (PHITS 3.34)

The Specific Absorbed Fractions (SAFs) displayed in this explorer were simulated using the ICRP 145 Adult Male Mesh Phantom (MRCP-AM) [1,3].

By tracking radiation transport directly through tetrahedral mesh elements in the PHITS 3.34 Monte Carlo code [3], energy deposition from monoenergetic photons and secondary electrons is calculated with high spatial fidelity. For organs with multiple segmented regions (such as kidneys with cortex, medulla, and pelvis), the total organ SAF is evaluated via a mass-weighted average of the subregion SAF values [3].
